newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to seek world backing in Moscow fleet row.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to seek world backing in Moscow fleet row.

text.p: Ukraine on Tuesday accused the Russian parliament of indulging in anti-Ukrainian behaviour and said it would appeal for help from the international community to solve a long dispute with Russia over the Black Sea fleet.
A foreign ministry statement lashed Russian deputies who plan on Wednesday to declare Sevastopol, the fleet headquarters on Ukraine's Crimean peninsula, a Russian territory.
"The actions of some deputies who want to adopt a resolution on Sevastopol's status have an anti-Ukrainian spirit," the statement said.
Last month Russia's State Duma voted to cancel the division of the fleet, agreed as part of moves to secure friendly bilateral relations after the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
The Russian government did not back the proposal, which was not legally binding.
A senior foreign ministry official said Kiev might appeal to the United Nations Security Council and complain to the Commonwealth of Independent States.

"We will react on both a bilateral and an international level as well as within international structures which deal with security problems," First Deputy Foreign Minister Anton Buteiko, told reporters in Kiev.

Ukrainian news agencies quoted Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko, who is accompanying President Leonid Kuchma on a visit to Greece, as saying that Kiev would seek support from the nuclear powers which guaranteed its territorial integrity when Ukraine agreed to give up its nuclear arms.
The United States, Britain, Russia and France signed a memorandum guaranteeing Ukraine's security and sovereignty in Budapest in December 1994, when Kiev vowed to disarm.
China also backed the deal through its foreign ministry.
Ukraine has since transferred more than 1,800 nuclear warheads to Russia for destruction.
The new upsurge in the fleet row appears to have upset prospects of signing a long-awaited keynote political accord between the two Slav states.
President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, promised Kuchma when they met in Moscow on October 24 that he would visit Kiev to sign a Friendship Treaty when he was better.

The two said they had solved all the problems over the dispute, which had led to Yeltsin postponing six trips to Kiev in 20 months and centres on agreeing elusive rental terms for Russia basing its ships in Sevastopol.

The Ukrainian parliament issued a clear warning to its Russian counterpart on Tuesday, scheduling a debate for next week on whether Russia should withdraw its entire 600-vessel share of the fleet from Crimea by the year 2000.

A round of talks between Russian and Ukrainian experts trying to complete documents for signing by Kuchma and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin last week ended without significant result, and the next round is yet to be scheduled.
Ukrainian and Russian media said on Tuesday that Chernomyrdin, who had been due to visit Kiev on November 15, had postponed the trip until a proper deal was agreed on the fleet.
